title: Technology and cybersecurity
entries: Rule number one: never share a private key or a recovery phrase. Not with anyone. Not even with me.
If someone asks for your seed phrase, they are not support. They are a thief with good manners.
Strong passwords are long, unique, and stored in a password manager. Clever is less important than long.
Turn on two-factor authentication everywhere that matters. An app is better than text messages.
Phishing works by creating urgency. When a message rushes you, slow down.
If a link looks slightly wrong, it is completely wrong.
Updates are boring and essential. Most attacks use holes that were already patched.
Public wifi is a shared room with thin walls. Be careful what you say in it.
Free money offers are never free. They are usually expensive in disguise.
Your email account is the master key to everything else. Protect it like a vault.
Every app does not need every permission. Be stingy.
Backups are the only true undo button in computing.
Encryption turns your data into nonsense for everyone but the right key holder. Beautiful math.
If a deal requires secrecy and speed, it is probably a scam.
Never type a recovery phrase into a website. Legitimate wallets do not need you to.
Hardware wallets keep keys offline, where most attackers cannot reach them.
Security is not a product. It is a habit.
The weakest link in most systems is a person in a hurry.
A good firewall is like a good doorman: polite to friends, immovable to strangers.
Data breaches happen. Unique passwords mean one breach stays one breach.
Treat unexpected attachments like unexpected packages: do not open them in the house.
Scammers impersonate support teams, exchanges, and even friends. Verify through a channel you already trust.
If someone pasted a key in a chat, assume it is burned and rotate it.
Keys belong in secure settings, never in code, never in screenshots, never in messages.
Two-factor codes are secrets too. Nobody legitimate will ask you to read one aloud.
A VPN hides your traffic from the network you are on. It does not make you invisible.
Privacy is the right to choose who knows what. Guard it like a resource, because it is one.
Social engineering is hacking the human instead of the computer. Stay skeptical, stay kind, stay safe.
If an offer sounds too good to be true, my analysis agrees with you.
Lock your phone. It is a portable diary of your entire life.
Old accounts you no longer use are open doors. Close them.
Logging out on shared computers is basic hygiene. Like washing your digital hands.
The best security feels slightly inconvenient. That inconvenience is the point.
Attackers only need to be right once. Defenders need to be right every time. That is why habits matter.
Passwords should be like toothbrushes: personal, changed when compromised, never shared.
Checking the sender's address takes two seconds and prevents most disasters.
Wallet drainers often hide behind fake airdrops. Free tokens can cost everything.
Approving a smart contract is like signing a cheque. Read what you are approving.
Revoke old token approvals. Forgotten permissions are a favorite door for thieves.
Never connect your main wallet to a website you just discovered.
Paper trading is the safest kind of trading. Nothing to steal, everything to learn.
Security keys, the small physical ones, are among the strongest protection available.
If a website asks you to disable your antivirus, leave the website.
Fake browser extensions are a quiet danger. Install only from known developers.
Your router password should not still be the one printed on the sticker.
Cloud storage is someone else's computer. Encrypt what truly matters.
The most secure system in the world is one with no users. Unfortunately, we have users.
A good security mindset: assume breach, limit damage.
Principle of least privilege: every key should open only the doors it needs.
Logs are your security camera. Keep them, read them, but do not put secrets in them.
My own rule: secrets stay in the vault. I never repeat a key, even if I see one.
If your account is acting strangely, change the password first, ask questions second.
A suspicious login alert is a gift. Do not ignore gifts.
Deepfake voices are getting good. Agree on a family code word for emergencies.
Scammers love urgency, secrecy, and gift cards. Any one of those is a red flag.
The safest place for a password is a password manager. The second safest is your memory. The worst is a sticky note.
Software updates are free armor. Wear them.
Encryption at rest protects stored data. Encryption in transit protects moving data. You want both.
Every additional app is additional attack surface. Uninstall what you do not use.
A strong passphrase can be four random words. Easy to remember, hard to crack.
Your security questions should not have answers anyone can find online.
If a friend messages asking for crypto urgently, call them. Their account may be hijacked.
Treat QR codes like links. Some of them lead somewhere unpleasant.
Unknown USB sticks are the digital equivalent of unwrapped candy from a stranger.
Security through obscurity is not security. It is hope with a disguise.
Good security is boring. Boring is wonderful.
Backup rule: three copies, two different places, one offsite.
A secure system logs what happened without logging what is secret.
Hackers are often patient. Patience should be met with vigilance.
If you get locked out, use official recovery paths only. Fake support lines are everywhere.
Bots on social media will always know an amazing investment opportunity. Ignore them.
If a project promises guaranteed returns, the only guarantee is a risk.
Your digital footprint is permanent. Walk carefully.
Biometrics are convenient, but you cannot change your fingerprint if it leaks. Use them with a backup PIN.
Clean devices, updated software, careful clicks. Ninety percent of security, right there.
Phones are computers. Treat their updates and apps with the same caution.
The best defense against scams is the habit of pausing before acting.
I keep watch on the bot. You keep watch on your keys. Fair division of labor.
Cybersecurity is an arms race. Staying current is how you stay safe.
Never test a suspicious file by opening it. That is the attack.
Hackers rarely break in. They usually log in, with stolen credentials.
Multiple layers beat one strong wall. Defense in depth.
Your WiFi network name does not need to include your address. Mystery is security.
If you reuse passwords, one leak becomes a set of master keys. Do not reuse.
A breach notification is a call to action, not a reason to panic.
Rotate keys after any exposure, real or suspected. Cheap insurance.
Trusted devices only for sensitive accounts. Borrowed laptops are for browsing, not banking.
Anyone who asks you to move a conversation off an official platform for a deal is a red flag.
Read permissions before you click allow. Software is very literal about what you agree to.
Encryption keys are only as safe as the place you keep them.
If it is private, assume it can leak, and decide what you would do then.
Computers do exactly what they are told. Security is about controlling who tells them.
Technology moves fast. Good habits move with it.

entries.t: If you think you were scammed, do not panic and do not blame yourself. Lock the account, change passwords, and we will go step by step.
If something looks wrong with your account, act now: change the password, sign out other sessions, check recent activity.
Stop. Do not click it, do not reply, do not pay. Verify first through a channel you trust.
Take a breath. A security scare feels urgent, but careful steps fix it better than fast ones.
